subject: Agriculture
title: Soil Horizons
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Soil Horizons.

hook.text: Dig a pit in the ground and you'll see layers—each a different color, texture, and story.

buildup.text: The O horizon sits on top: leaf litter, dead plants, and decomposing organic matter.

discovery.text: Below that, the A horizon—topsoil—is where most roots grow and most farming happens.

twist.text: The B horizon collects minerals washed down from above. It's dense, often clay-rich, and hard to dig.

climax.text: At the bottom, the C horizon is barely weathered rock—the raw material for future soil above it.

punchline.text: Soil tells its history in layers, if you dig deep enough.

quiz.question: Which soil horizon is most important for farming?

details.summary: Soil horizons are distinct layers visible in a cross-section of soil, each with different properties. This topic covers the O, A, B, and C horizons, how they form through the movement of water and materials, and what they reveal about soil health and history.
details.whyItMatters: Reading soil horizons is like reading geological history. The thickness and composition of each horizon tell farmers about drainage, fertility, root depth potential, and whether soil has been degraded by erosion or compaction.
takeaways: Soil profiles typically show O (organic), A (topsoil), B (subsoil), and C (parent material) horizons
The A horizon contains most organic matter and biological activity critical for crops
Horizon thickness and color reveal drainage patterns, fertility, and erosion history

faq.question: What are the main soil horizons and what do they contain?
faq.answer: The O horizon is decomposing organic matter on the surface. The A horizon (topsoil) is the darkest, most fertile layer where roots concentrate. The B horizon (subsoil) accumulates clay and minerals washed down from above. The C horizon is partially weathered parent rock.

faq.question: How do soil horizons form over time?
faq.answer: Rain percolating downward dissolves and carries clay particles, organic acids, and minerals from upper layers into lower ones—a process called eluviation. Organic litter accumulates on top, organisms mix it into the A horizon, and clay accumulates in the B horizon, creating distinct layers.
